claims.text: At stage-2, PlaceOrderAsync creates the Order, calls repository.AddAsync(order), then notifier.Send(order, "order placed"), then one repository.SaveChangesAsync(); CancelOrderAsync and ShipOrderAsync also call Send before SaveChangesAsync.
At stage-2 INotifier.Send takes the Order itself (void Send(Order order, string subject)), and DI registers QueuedNotifier as the scoped INotifier.

QueuedNotifier.Send only calls db.Notifications.Add with a Notification (Order = order, Channel "email", Status "pending", CreatedAt and NextAttemptAt = now); it saves nothing and contacts no mail server.
DbSet.Add only begins tracking the entity in the Added state; it is inserted when SaveChanges is called.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Basic Save (Adding Data); DbSet<TEntity>.Add API

claims.text: By default, SaveChanges applies all tracked changes in one database transaction: if any change fails, the transaction is rolled back and none are applied. Hence every order placed from stage-2 on has its notifications row.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Transactions (default transaction behavior)

claims.text: DonHangDbContext is registered with AddDbContext (scoped), so within one request QueuedNotifier and EfOrderRepository receive the same DbContext instance.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: DbContext in dependency injection (AddDbContext registers scoped); ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:17-25 @ stage-2

claims.text: Setting the navigation Order = order lets EF Core fill notifications.order_id from the order's generated id when it saves both in the same SaveChanges.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Saving related data (adding a graph of new entities; FK set from principal key)

claims.text: orders.id is generated by PostgreSQL during the INSERT, so the order has no id when Send is called before SaveChangesAsync.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Generated values (keys); prereq backend.l1.saving-changes

claims.text: From stage-2, notifications has columns status (CHECK pending/sent/failed), attempts, created_at, next_attempt_at and nullable sent_at, and a foreign key order_id -> orders.id.
OrdersController.Create returns CreatedAtAction (201) after PlaceOrderAsync returns; nothing in that path calls IEmailSender or the mail server.

NotificationSender is the only code that reads jobs from notifications: each round, ClaimDueAsync selects rows with status 'pending' and next_attempt_at <= now (due); a new job's next_attempt_at is the current time.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: DonHang.Infrastructure/NotificationQueue.cs:16-30; NotificationSender.cs:47-59; git grep ClaimDueAsync

claims.text: SendOneAsync calls email.SendAsync, then sets notification.Status = "sent" and notification.SentAt; CompleteAsync saves the round's changes with SaveChangesAsync and commits.
The mailpit service in docker-compose.yml is a fake mail server that accepts every email the api sends over SMTP (mailpit:1025) and delivers none; its HTTP API on port 8025 shows what arrived.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang @ stage-2: docker-compose.yml mailpit service and comment; Mailpit docs (SMTP testing server, API)

claims.text: A row still pending when the api process stops remains pending in PostgreSQL, and the sender picks it up in its first rounds after the start (ClaimDueAsync filters only on status and next_attempt_at, up to 10 rows per round).
claims.source_hint: NotificationQueue.cs:16-30 @ stage-2; PostgreSQL docs: committed data is durable

claims.text: The email is sent on the sender's next tick (PeriodicTimer of 2 s), so it goes out a few seconds after the order response, not at the same moment.
claims.source_hint: NotificationSender.cs:13,25-39 @ stage-2; outputs/stage-2/scripts/backend/order-email.txt ('sent after the response came back: yes')

claims.text: If the process stops between two separate SaveChangesAsync calls, the first transaction is committed and the second never runs, leaving an order without its notifications row.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Transactions (each SaveChanges call uses its own transaction by default)

claims.text: order-email.sh (run from the host, it executes inside the lab box) places an order as customer 1 (anh.tran@example.com) and prints -> 201, 'email | order placed', 'status after the sender's next round: sent', 'sent after the response came back: yes' and Mailpit's from/to/subject.
Keeping the job in the database is preferable to an in-memory list when the job must survive a restart or deploy; the cost is a delay of up to one timer interval.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs: Background tasks with hosted services (queued background tasks are in-memory); lesson reasoning
